related_questions.question: Can lung cancer nodules be cured?
related_questions.snippet: Cancerous lung nodules are often treated with surgery when they are caught in an early stage when they are small and have not spread to other parts of the body. Lung nodules found in later stages may be treated with a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and targeted therapy.

related_questions.question: What is the survival rate of cancerous lung nodules?
related_questions.snippet: About 40 percent of pulmonary nodules turn out to be cancerous. Half of all patients treated for a cancerous pulmonary nodule live at least five years past the diagnosis. But if the nodule is one centimeter across or smaller, survival after five years rises to 80 percent. That's why early detection is critical.

related_questions.question: What happens if you have a nodule on your lung?

text_blocks.snippet: A lung nodule, a small spot on the lung, is often found incidentally on imaging scans and is usually benign. However, some nodules can be cancerous, so further investigation is often needed to determine the nature of the nodule. Depending on the size, appearance, and risk factors (like smoking history), doctors may recommend monitoring with repeat scans, or further testing such as a biopsy.

list.snippet: A lung nodule is a small, roundish spot on the lung that appears denser than the surrounding tissue on a chest X-ray or CT scan.
Most lung nodules are benign, meaning they are not cancerous.
Some common causes of benign nodules include:
Previous lung infections (like pneumonia) or inflammation.
Scar tissue.
Fungal infections.
Autoimmune diseases.
Exposure to dust or chemicals.

text_blocks.snippet: What happens if a lung nodule is found?

list.title: Initial assessment:
list.snippet: Doctors will first assess the size, shape, and appearance of the nodule on imaging and evaluate the patient's risk factors (like smoking history, age, family history).

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: For small, low-risk nodules, the most common approach is to repeat the CT scan at intervals (e.g., 3 months, 6 months, 1 year) to monitor for any changes in size or appearance.

list.title: Further testing:
list.snippet: If the nodule is large, looks suspicious, or the patient has significant risk factors, further testing may be needed. This may include:
CT-guided biopsy: A needle is guided by CT to sample tissue from the nodule.
Bronchoscopy: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is inserted into the airways to visualize the nodule and potentially take a biopsy.
PET scan: A scan that can help determine if the nodule is cancerous.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: If the nodule is determined to be cancerous, treatment options may include:
Surgery: To remove the nodule or affected lung tissue.
Radiation therapy: To kill cancer cells.
Chemotherapy: To kill cancer cells, often used in conjunction with other treatments.
Most lung nodules are not cancerous.
Early detection of lung cancer through lung nodule screening can lead to more effective treatment and better outcomes.
If you have been diagnosed with a lung nodule, follow your doctor's recommendations for monitoring and treatment.

related_questions.question: Is cancer in the lungs curable?

text_blocks.snippet: While not all lung cancers are curable, some types, particularly when caught early, can be cured with treatment. Early detection significantly improves the chances of successful treatment and cure.

list.title: Early Detection is Key:
list.snippet: If lung cancer is discovered when it's still localized to the lung and hasn't spread, it has a higher chance of being cured.

list.title: Treatment Options:
list.snippet: Treatment for lung cancer can include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapies.

list.title: Remission vs. Cure:
list.snippet: While "cure" isn't always used, doctors often use terms like "remission" or "no evidence of disease" (NED) to describe a situation where the cancer is undetectable after treatment.

list.title: Survival Rates:
list.snippet: Survival rates vary widely depending on the stage of the cancer at diagnosis.

list.title: Advanced Lung Cancer:
list.snippet: If lung cancer has spread to other parts of the body, it's often not considered curable, and treatment focuses on managing symptoms and prolonging life.

list.title: Small Cell Lung Cancer:
list.snippet: Small cell lung cancer is often treated with chemotherapy and radiation therapy due to its tendency to spread quickly.

list.title: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer:
list.snippet: Non-small cell lung cancer can be curable with surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation if caught early.

list.title: Advances in Treatment:
list.snippet: Newer treatments and targeted therapies are improving survival rates and quality of life for lung cancer patients.
